Karen Murphy University of Maryland The purpose for this research was threefold: to determine whether distinct and informative student profiles would emerge from knowledge, interest, and strategy measures specific to educational psychology; to compare these profiles with prior studies; and to explore changes in student profiles across an academic semester
As a result of cluster-analytic procedures, 3 distinct groups of participants emerged at pretest, and 4 emerged at posttest
One of the profiles that remained fairly consistent from pretest to posttest was the Learning-Oriented cluster
Students fitting this profile began the semester with the highest means in interest and strategic processing and with a moderate level of domain knowledge

By the end of the semester, this cluster obtained the highest means also on the domain knowledge test Yet, the largest cluster at posttest seemed unable or unwilling to learn from demanding exposition
In the last decade, the research on individual differences has moved toward the exploration of intraindividual variabili- ties (Ackerman, Kyllonen, & Roberts, in press)

That is to say, researchers have become increasingly concerned with how cognitive and noncognitive factors, such as knowledge and self-regulation, configure differently within individuals (Ackerman, Kanfer, & Goff, 1995)
Our purpose in this study was to explore such intraindividual diiferences by examining the various learner profiles that emerged within one classroom
Specifically, we wanted to ascertain whether undergraduates enrolled in an educational psychology course would naturally form into distinctive clusters based on their academic characteristics
We formed these clusters from information on students' subject matter knowledge, inter- ests, and strategic processing
Because they were con- structed by means of cluster analysis, the resulting profiles encompassed not only multiple indicators for each student but also data from every participating student

In addition, we set out to compare the academic profiles in this study with other characterizations in the literature, to examine their consistency (e.g., de Jong & Ferguson- Hessler, 1986; Renkl, 1997)
If the clusterings we detected manifested similarities to profiles reported in related research, then their diagnostic and instructional relevance would seemingly be augmented
Thus, it was important to us not only whether such profiles could be statistically verified but also whether they would be instruc- tionally valuable

As educators, our assumption is that formal learning positively affects participating students

Tracking any shifts in student profiles from the beginning to the end of the semester would offer clues to the potential impact school-based experiences have on mature learners' knowledge, interests, and strategic processing

Our expectation was that instruction over time should create greater diversity among our students in terms of their knowledge, interest, and strategic behavior, particularly because most students enter this learning environment as relative novices

For instance, one might predict that a clustering of students who begin instruction with some knowledge and interest in the content, and with the ability to perform strategically, would have an advantage over those who initially have little knowledge or interest in the subject matter, or who must struggle to learn new or demanding information (Alexander, 1997)
Should such profiles exist, then the differences among them might well be magnified by a semester of study (Stanovich, 1986)

A rise in the mean differences for knowledge, interest, and strategic processing among clusters from the outset to the conclusion of a course would be indicative of this type of fan-spread effect (Bryk & Weisberg, 1977)
Equally interesting, the interaction be- tween the cognitive and motivational measures might well vary among the different clusters from pretest to posttest
In essence, not only would the mean scores differ among clusters but the correlational patterns would vary as well
We chose knowledge, interest, and strategic processing as our clustering variables in this study for several reasons

First, it can be argued that one of the central aims of schooling is the construction of principled knowledge about ftmdamental academic domains or disciplines (Alexander, Murphy, & Woods, 1996; Gelman & Greeno, 1989)
We expect that students who participate in formal instruction for 12 or more years will garner a body of relevant and usable knowledge in such fields as mathematics, science, history, and reading
436 ALEXANDER AND MURPHY this corpus of knowledge specific to a particular field of study (Alexander, Schallert, & Hare, 1991)

Yet researchers have found that those who attain compe- tence or reach expertise in any given field not only are knowledgeable but also manifest a strong personal interest or investment in that domain (e.g., Guthrie & Wigfield, 1997; Mitchell, 1993; Renninger, 1992)
In addition, they are skilled in reasoning and problem solving (e.g., Alex- ander, Graham, & Harris, in press; Holyoak, 1991; Pirolli & Recker, 1994)

Through our research on academic develop- ment, the perception that competence and expertise are better understood as a multidimensional interplay of knowl- edge, interest, and strategic components repeatedly has been reinforced (e.g., Alexander, 1997; Alexander, Kulikowich, & Schulze, 1994; Alexander, Murphy, Woods, Duhon, & Parker, 1997)

Because of these presumed linkages, we used measures of personal or individual interest (Hidi, 1990; Schiefele, 1991) and strategic processing (Pressley, Borkowski, & Schneider, 1989; Pressley et al., 1992; Weinstein & Mayer, 1986), along with a domain knowledge task, to build our learner profiles in this study
With this choice of clustering variables, what kind of profiles might we expect in a classroom of undergraduates studying educational psychology

Research on problem solving (e.g., Recker & Pirolli, 1995; Renkl, 1997) and expert-novice distinctions (e.g., Chi, Bassok, Lewis, Reimann, & Glaser, 1989; de Jong & Ferguson-Hessler, 1986) provided us clues as to the potential intraindividual differences we might anticipate
These cluster-analytic stud- ies were conducted across various domains (e.g., physics, programming, and mathematics) and involved learners of differing ages and varied abilities

Thus, even though studies in these areas did not incorporate motivational measures and rarely included dedicated measures of strategic processing, they still produced some important and consistent groupings that informed the present investigation
In particular, several studies identified important charac- teristics of more successful versus less successful perform- ers

For instance, individuals who were generally successful at task performance either (a) had the benefit of a substantial body of relevant domain knowledge on which they relied or (b) appeared to overcome lower levels of domain knowledge through marked effort and effective strategic behavior (Recker & Pirolli, 1995)
Renkl (1997) referred to the former group of successful performers as anticipative reason- ers and the latter clustering as principle-based explainers
In contrast, students who were novice or poor in their problem solving seemed to treat the given task or problem in a cursory manner
As a result, they failed to deal with its inherent structure or complexity (e.g., Chi et al., 1989; de Jong & Ferguson-Hessler, 1986, 1991)
Other less successful students appeared to recognize the limitations of their performance but apparently did not take advantage of available resources or did not use compensatory strategies
Students matching this particular profile were described as passive learners (Recker & Pirolli, 1995; Renkl, 1997)

Thus, the research on problem solving and expert-novice differences suggests that students within classrooms can bedistinguished on the basis of the relevant knowledge they may or may not possess and of their ability and willingness to engage in the effortful and strategic processing of a challenging task
In a recent study, Alexander, Jetton, and Kulilowich (1995) profiled students' academic learning in the field of human biology-immunology also by means of cluster analysis
(1995) included a measure of student interest, along with gauges of domain knowledge and strategic processing

Participants included premedical students and students in an educational psychology graduate program (Experiment 1), as well as undergraduates enrolled in an introductory educational psychology class (Experi- ment 2)
Several informative clusters, with similarities to those described, emerged across the two experiments
In general, we would characterize these as low, high, and mixed profiles

For instance, the low-profile group, who scored the lowest performance on the criterion measure (i.e., text comprehension task), knew little and reportedly cared little about the domain and had difficulties recalling what they had read
This low-profile group seems similar to the passive and superficial groups in the Recker and Pirolli (1995) and Renkl (1997) studies
The high-profile cluster, by comparison, were (a) most knowledgeable in human biology-immunology, (b) most interested in that field, and (c) skilled at learning from demanding texts
This cluster has the most in common with the experts or good problem solvers in the Chi et al
Between these two clusters was a mixed profile, consisting of skillful novices who seemed rather capable of learning from demanding exposition but still knew little about human biology-immunology
This group parallels the principle-based explainers in Renkl's (1997) study, who also overcame their initial deficits in knowledge to perform well on the task

(1995) found another mixed cluster of undergraduates who had an ad- equate base of subject matter knowledge but did not perform particularly well when reading or recalling challenging subject matter text
According to the researchers, the poor performance of this particular cluster could be the result of either an inability or an unwillingness to apply appropriate text-processing strategies
Thus, with these prior studies as a backdrop, we set out to extend the research in several ways
Certainly, cluster analysis has shown promise in separating more successful from less successful learners in scientific and mathematical domains

However, this ap- proach has not been as frequently applied in domains, like educational psychology, that are more ill structured (i.e., less procedurally rich or problem based) in nature (Alexander, 1992; Spiro, Coulson, Feltovich, & Anderson, 1994; Spiro & Jehng, 1990)
Second, our intention was to allow domain knowledge to vary freely—neither to exacerbate its effects nor diminish the role it might play for these students
For instance, certain researchers selected participants thought to be quite distinct in their knowledge base, as in the case of experts

LEARNER PROFILES 437 versus novices (Chi et al., 1989), good versus poor problem solvers (de Jong & Ferguson-Hessler, 1986), or premedical versus non-premedical students (Alexander et al., 1995, Experiment 1)
Conversely, other researchers used novel and challenging tasks they believed would lessen the impact of prior knowledge (Renkl, 1997)
Finally, we set out to explore changes that might result in student profiles after formal instruction in the field of educational psychology
The prior studies that guided our thinking had not consid- ered the possibility of shifts in learner profiles over time and, thus, left this important question unanswered
Method Participants The participants for this study were 329 students enrolled in an introductory course in educational psychology taught by Alex- ander
The course was a requirement for their certification in elementary and secondary teacher education
The majority of these students (approximately 80%) were juniors and seniors at a large university in the Southwest
The proportion of women and men in the sample was typical for teacher education programs (i.e., 280 women and 49 men)
Most participants (92%) were Caucasian, with a small percentage of Hispanic (6%) and African American (2%) students

Clustering Measures Because we were concerned with the ecological validity of the procedures that would result in the learner profiles, we adminis- tered the battery of measures described herein at the outset and the conclusion of the course under the following conditions

At pretest, students were informed that their performance on these measures would not be reflected in their course grade but would be used to modify the existing curriculum in accordance with their demon- strated strengths and weaknesses
At posttest, students' perfor- mance on the various knowledge, interest, and strategy tasks was part of their final examination
In this manner, we believed that the students would approach the tasks as relevant components of the course and not as experimental measures that were tangential to their learning and performance

In constructing a measure of domain knowledge, we wanted an instrument that would afford us a picture of students' breadth of knowledge in the field of educational psychology versus their depth of understanding of selected con- cepts, procedures, or topics (cf
We developed items from the instructional materials for the course and the required text (Goetz, Alexander, & Ash, 1992)
Sixteen items were multiple-choice questions, and 8 were commonality items (i.e., items for which students had to identify a superordinate term for four given terms)
Examples are provided in prior research (e.g., Alexander, Murphy, Woods, et al., 1997)
These items were dichotomously scored as correct or incorrect (highest possible score = 24)
The Kuder-Richardson 20 for the measure at pretest was .62, We considered this to be an acceptable level of reliability, given the relatively low variability of scores (M = 12.66, SD = 2.26)
Our measure of student interest was a 26-item scale that tapped students' interest in concepts associated with the domain of educational psychology
Students indicated their interest in these concepts on a 7-point rating scale, ranging from 1 (not veryinterested) to 7 (very interested)
They were also given the option of indicating that they were "uncertain of the meaning" of a particular concept or topic
We considered the terms on the scale to be representative of central concepts within the domain (e.g., memory, problem solving, teacher-made tests, and learned helpless- ness)
Moreover, these concepts were addressed within the course text and class discussions
The Cronbach alpha for the scale (highest possible score = 182) was .82
Our strategic processing dimension in the profiles was represented by two measures that the students completed in conjunction, a strategy-use inventory and a recall task
Specifically, students studied a given text and maintained a record of the strategies they used during the process (strategy-use inventory)
Then, after studying, the students answered two ques- tions about the passage content (recall task)
For both of these measures, we considered the choice of texts to be a significant factor
Not only did we want the content to be relevant to the course but we also wanted the texts to be sufficiently lengthy and challenging to warrant strategic effort

Using these criteria, we chose two passages from a review of research dealing with the Learner-Centered Psychological Principles (American Psychological Association, Presidential Task Force on Psychology in Education, 1993), which we had authored (Alexander & Murphy, 1998)
The knowledge passage consisted of 1,025 words, 85 sentences, and 10 paragraphs
The motivation passage was 1,126 words, 93 sentences, and 9 paragraphs in length
Each student read one of the passages, presented in counterbalanced order, at pretest and the other at posttest
Before they read, we informed the students mat they would answer questions about the passages when they completed their studying
They were then allowed to read and study the passages for as long as they wanted
After studying the passage and before the recall task, students were presented with an intervening task (i.e., long-division math problem)
The first question asked students to write down any important information they could remember from the passage
For the sake of this analysis, we combined students' answers to these two questions into one recall score
To aid us in scoring, we constructed a response protocol for each text
These protocols were essentially checklists containing gist statements for each of the sentences in the passages (85 for the knowledge passage and 93 for the motivation passage)
For example, one sentence in the knowledge text read, "In essence, the knowledge base is the total of all an individual knows or believes" (Alexander et al., 1991)

We indicated this sentence on the protocol with the phrase "knowledge base = all one knows/believes." When it came to scoring students* recalls, we checked their written responses against the protocol to gauge whether the information listed was (a) in the text and (b) an accurate rendering of the content
Even though some students, included the same idea in their answers to both questions, we counted an entry only once
To determine the recall score, we simply tallied the number of marks received for the two questions

In the past, we have developed response protocols in which each entry signified an idea unit roughly equivalent to a subordinate clause or phrase conveying a complete thought (Pichert & Ander- son, 1977)
However, given the length of the chosen texts and the general nature of the questions that we asked, we did not consider this level of specificity necessary for scoring students' recalls in mis study
Interrater reliability for scoring the recall task was .92, with any differences resolved in discussion

As they studied the texts, students were instructed to monitor their strategy use
The inventory, which consisted of 15 general text- processing strategies, had been used in prior research (a = .80; Knight & Alexander, 1994)
We submitted the pretest data to a common factor analysis to extract the underlying structure of the inventory
An eigenvalue of 1 served as the criterion for retaining a factor, whereas a loading of .40 or greater was the standard for retaining a strategy within a particular factor
By means of the orthogonal varimax procedure, four factors emerged that we found to be theoretically and statistically justifiable

Strategies within Factor 1 appear related to the active processing of the text (i.e., image, link to background knowledge, make predictions, use self-questioning, ignore noncritical words, and look for salient details)

Factor 2 strategies apparently were those procedures students used to process the text at a more surface level (i.e., reread parts of the text, change reading rate, and use the context to determine meaning)

Factor 3 seemed to have more to do with identifying the gist or main ideas contained in the passage (i.e., rehearse the main ideas, elaborate main ideas, reflect on the reading, and summarize mentally)
What unified the strategies in Factor 4 was that they were virtually unused by students as they studied the passages at pretest (i.e., consult reference materials and look up vocabulary)

These four factors explained 42% of the variance in reported strategy use at pretest Important factors, such as prior knowledge and a willingness to engage in strategic processing, may also have contributed to students' reported strategy use
On the inventory, students were directed to checkmark any strategy that they used to comprehend and remember the passage
When they finished, they placed an asterisk next to those strategies they considered most helpful
Students received 0 points for any unmarked strategy, 1 point for all checked strategies, and 2 points for those they asterisked (maximum score = 30)
As with the knowledge measure, we attribute this moderate reliability to low variability among participants at pretest
Also at pretest, a number of strategies were unused by the students, thereby constraining the range of scores
Criterion Measure As the external criterion on which we built our student profiles, we selected a domain-specific analogy task
This task consisted of eight classic or simple problems of the form A:B::C:D (e.g., Pavlov: classical conditioning::Skinner:<?p£ra«r conditioning)
The content for these problems, as with other measures in our battery, was taken directly from material covered during the semester
We originally had conceived of the analogy task as one component ofthe domain knowledge variable
However, subsequent review and analysis convinced us that this task would serve well as the outcome measure in this study for theoretical and statistical reasons

From a theoretical standpoint, there is an ample literature indicating that successful performance on verbal analogy problems (Embretson, 1983; Goswami, 1992; Sternberg & Rifkin, 1979), including those specific to a domain of study (Alexander, Murphy, & Speri, 1997; White & Alexander, 1986), require both conceptual knowledge and strategic capability
Thus, the use of an analogy task afforded us an outcome measure that encompassed two central dimensions within our profiles: domain knowledge and strategic processing

Further, on the basis of a confirmatory factor analysis by means of structural equation modeling (AMOS; Arbuckle, 1997), this analogy task was found to be a highly valid measure of domain-specific analogical reasoning (see Alexander, Murphy, & Kulikowich, 1998, for indices of fit)

The scoring of these items followed a categorization scheme that has been validated in prior studies by means of multidimensional scaling (Alexander, 1990) and item response theory (Alexander, Murphy, & Kulikowich, 1998)
The interrater reliability for the scoring of the analogy task was .98
We, along with a doctoral student, determined this rate by independently coding the responses for 33 (10%) randomly selected participants
Because of the high level of agreement (Engelhard, 1996), the remaining items were scored by Murphy only
These response categories were hierarchi- cally ordered on the basis of the knowledge and strategic capability each was assumed to convey (see Table 1)

For example, Category 3 (Nondomain) errors covered student responses that fell outside of the target domain, educational psychology (e.g., Pavlov: classical conditioning: :Skinner: romantic conditioning)
Category 5 (Do- main) errors, by comparison, demonstrated student's ability to produce a response from educational psychology (e.g., Pavlov: classical conditioning::Skinner: reinforcement)

Alexander, Murphy, and Kulikowich (1998) found not only that these response categories were hierarchical across respondents but also that students tended to display certain error patterns in their solutions
Because of the specificity at which student responses could be marked using this categorization scheme, we applied a partial-credit scoring model (Masters, 1982)
That is, we awarded 1 point for a Nonresponse (Category 1) to 7 points for a Correct Response (Category 7)

First, students' scores on all variables increased significantly from pretest to posttest
Increases in knowledge, interest, strategy use, and recall might well be expected after a semester of formal instruction in educational psychology
However, there is no direct way to ascribe causality in this study

Still, in light of the 15-week delay between pretest and posttest, it is unlikely that these significant changes can be attributed simply to a test-retest effect (see Willson & Putnam, 1982, for an extended discussion of pretest sensitization effects)
Second, we found that the analogical reasoning variable displayed the greatest increase from pretest to posttest, f(328) = 51.74,/

Because measures of analogical reasoning are frequently used as indicators of intelligence or cognitive aptitude, due in part to strong test-retest reliabili- ties (e.g., Goswami, 1992; Klix, 1992; Steinberg, 1977), we posited that this significant change was attributable in some measure to the instruction students received

What was relevant about this instruction was that it focused not only on strategic processes (e.g., inferring, mapping) associated with analogical reasoning (e.g., Alexander, White, Haensly, & Crimmins-Jeanes, 1987; Sternberg, 1977) but also on do- main concepts to which these processes were applied

Thus, by bringing their enhanced domain-specific knowledge and strategic processes to bear collectively on this task, students may have been able to register significant improvement from pretest to posttest
This trend in the data supported our choice of the analogy task as the external criterion for the cluster analysis
Despite these recorded increases from pretest to posttest, students' scores on the cognitive and motivational measures, especially at pretest, were typically low to moderate
Only the interest ratings could be considered somewhat high at the outset of the course
The lowest relative scores occurred for the strategy use and recall measures
At pretest, students tended to rely on rereading and similar surface-level process- ing strategies (e.g., changing reading rate) to guide their studying
The result was an average of less than 4 idea units recalled out of a possible 85 or 93
Many recall tasks call on students to write down everything they can remember from a given passage
In this case, students were told to list the"important" information from the passages
Not only did the average number of recalled idea units double at posttest but there were also quantitative and qualitative differences in students' strategy use
Specifically, the moderate rise in reported strategies was complemented by the fact that students marked more strategies that pertained to active processing or to identifying main ideas
In effect, students seemed to rely more on deeper processing strategies (e.g., summarizing) than surface-level ones (e.g., rereading) by the conclusion of the course
The preference for such strategies also seems in keeping with the nature of the recall task
(in press) recently argued that such a quantitative-qualitative shift in learners' strategy use could be viewed as evidence of growth in strategic processing
Cluster Analysis As noted, we used cluster analysis to detect emergent profiles in the domain of educational psychology
Milligan and Cooper (1987) recommended a technique in which one variable, an external criterion, is used to validate the differences among profiles
We chose analogical reasoning as that external criterion for the reasons previously stated
With analogical reasoning as the external criterion and domain knowledge, interest, strategy use, and recall as the clustering measures, we examined students' pretest and posttest profiles
Specifically, we used Ward's minimum- variance hierarchical clustering technique (Everitt, 1993; Ward, 1963)
In this analysis, differences in analogical reasoning ability served as an independent indicator of cluster-group distinctions
In effect, the relationship be- tween cluster profiles and the external criterion variable functions as a measure of convergent validity
We viewed the pretest phase of this research as somewhat confirmatory, due to the availability of relevant cluster-analytic studies in the literature against which to compare our resulting pro- files

However, our attempts to examine student profiles at posttest, and certainly our consideration of the role of formal instruction in contributing to such profiles, should be judged as rather exploratory

That is to say, this procedure starts with every individual representing a unique cluster and then continues to examine distances between clusters in a stepwise fashion until all individuals (i.e., response vectors) have been grouped into one cluster
In this study, distance was a measure of dissimilarity between two individuals given their responses on the knowledge, interest, and recall measures
Finally, we used dendrograms to aid our interpretation of the resulting clusters (Olson & Biolsi, 1991)
In these dendrograms, the number of meaningful clusters is based on an identification of the largest gaps or distances between cluster groups
Two such gaps emerged in the dendrogram at pretest and three at posttest

These results suggest that three student profiles could statistically account for academic performance at the outset of the semester, whereas four distinct clusters were required to capture student perfor- mance at posttest
At pretest, the emerging clusters bore similarities to those we identified in the literature
Descriptions of the Pretest Clusters The means and standard deviations for the criterion and clustering variables for the three pretest clusters are shown in Table 3
To understand the differences among these clusters, we first conducted a multivariate analysis of variance (MANOVA)
For this analysis, cluster group was the independent variable, and domain knowledge, interest, strategy use, and recall were the dependent variables
Results indicated a significant overall difference between clusters, F(10, 642) = 54.71,p < .0001
We followed this omnibus test with univariate analyses of variance (ANOVAs) for the four dependent variables and for the external criterion variable, analogical reasoning
The cluster groups were significantly different on all dependent measures, F(2, 328)s 35.64,p < .00001, MSB ^ 333.10
Performance on the analogical reasoning task also differed significantly for the clusters, F(2, 328) = 4.44,p < .01, MSE = 60.65

Next, to obtain a better understanding of the significant univariate effects among the three cluster groups, we conducted a series of multiple comparisons by Fisher's(1935) least significant difference (LSD) procedure
We chose Fisher's LSD procedure (a = .05) because it exhibits higher statistical power when compared with other multiple comparison tests (e.g., Levin, Serlin, & Seaman, 1994)
The results of these between-cluster comparisons are presented in Table 3 as subscript designations
We consider these differences in the general descriptions of the three clusters that follow
On the bases of their attributes, we refer to those three as the Learning-Oriented, Strong-Knowledge, and Low-Profile clusters
Finally, we performed a discriminant function analysis, to validate the presumed multidimensional character of the clusters

This analysis would provide support for the notion that the emerging clusters arose from an interplay of cognitive and motivational variables (e.g., recall and inter- est) and could not be attributed to differences in a single construct (e.g., knowledge)
For this discriminant function analysis, performance on the analogical reasoning, knowl- edge, interest, strategy use, and recall measures was used to predict group membership
Results demonstrated that over- all group membership was accurately predicted for 84% of cases
The highest prediction accuracy occurred for the Strong-Knowledge group (88.2%), followed by the Low- Profile and the Learning-Oriented clusters (83% and 82.4%, respectively)
As a last step in this analysis, we calculated Cohen's kappa, to determine the percentage of correct classification over and above what would be expected due to chance
Collec- tively, these analyses provide strong support for the conten- tion that the three clusters that emerged at pretest were not only statistically unique but also multidimensional in nature
What seemed to distinguish the Learning-Oriented cluster (n = 108) was that students displayed an initially moderate level of domain knowledge with a high level of domain-specific interest
They appeared to engage in the most effortful processing of the knowledge and motivation passages also and, subsequently, remem- bered the most from those passages relative to the other clusters
In addition, they recorded one of the highest means on the analogical reasoning task at pretest

It is for this reason that we refer to them as learning oriented; that is, reflecting a learning or mastery goal orientation (e.g., Dweck & Leggett, 1988; Meece & Holt, 1993)
Overall, this cluster is closest to the high- knowledge-high-interest group, which led performance in the Alexander et al
(1995) experiments, or to the highly successful principle-based reasoners in the Renkl (1997) research
By comparison, students in the Strong-Knowledge group (n = 68) apparently began the course with more relevant knowledge than those in other clusters
These students tended also to rely on that existing knowledge to guide their performance
These students' interest in educational psychology, by comparison, was the lowest of the three clusters, and their strategic efforts, as well as their passage recalls, were rather moderate
Comparable profiles have been reported by others (e.g., de Jong & Ferguson-Hessler, 1986; Recker & Pirolli, 1995; Renkl 1997)
As was true in these prior studies, students fitting this profile were still able to perform successfully on the outcome measures at the beginning of the term

It would seem, therefore, that a relevant body of subject-matter knowledge could potentially compensate for limited interest and moderate effort after meaning, at least in the initial stages of domain learning (Alexander, 1997)
The largest cluster at pretest, the Low-Profile group (n = 153), reported only a moderate interest in the domain of educational psychology and were seemingly the least informed in this domain
Further, these students used the least number of strategies and remembered the least of the three clusters
Likewise, they were signifi- cantly below the other two clusters on the criterion task
These relatively low scores in analogical reasoning seem understandable in the light of students' performance on the associated knowledge and strategy tasks
This Low-Profile group is analogous to the low-profile cluster in the Alex- ander et al
(1995) study and to the passive and superficial processors described by Recker and Pirolli (1995)

It is understandable that such a large portion of students would fall into this Low-Profile group before formal instruction in educational psychology or in strategic processing.Descriptions of the Posttest Clusters After approximately 15 weeks of explicit instruction in the domain, along with the discussion and practice of various learning and studying strategies, our participants fell into four distinct clusters

As we did at pretest, we first examined the differences among these groups by means of MANOVA, with cluster group as the independent variable and the knowledge, interest, strategy use, and recall mea- sures as dependent variables
The outcome indicated an overall difference among the clusters, F(\2, 962) = 46.93,p < .0001

The univariate ANOVAs we conducted showed that the four clusters varied significantly with regard to their domain knowledge, interest, strategy use, and passage recall, F(3, 328) > 23.41,p < .00001, MSE == 179.40

Several researchers have suggested that knowledge and individual interest are significantly corre- lated, in that those with the greatest knowledge are likewise personally invested in the domain (Alexander, 1997; Ren- ninger, 1992)
For most students in this study, that associa- tion between knowledge and interest was supported
How- ever, this was not the case for this particular group of students, who apparently did pretty well in a domain they cared relatively little about
What is quite interesting is what became of students who initially formed the Low- Profile cluster at pretest
Unlike the clusterings that emerged at pretest, there was no profile group that was consistently low on almost all cognitive and motivational dimensions
Rather, it appears that those 153 students in the Low-Profile group, along with others from the remaining clusters, re-formed into two contrasting profiles

First, there were those students (n = 76) who seemingly struggled very hard to learn the content, as indicated by their strategy use, and who even maintained a moderate level of interest in the domain
Yet, when it came to building a base of domain knowledge, these students were among the least successfullearners in the class

The high level of strategic effort might help to explain how this group, with the lowest average on the domain knowledge measure, was still able to perform moderately well on both the recall and analogy tasks
Perhaps these effortful processors learned to compensate for their limited domain knowledge by working more effortfully and more strategically
It is also possible that this group of students is simply less skilled at taking declarative knowledge measures, such as the domain knowledge task in this study
The profile for this group of students deviates from those in the literature
As evidenced from the labels attached to unsuccessful learners in prior studies (e.g., passive or superficial), low performance is attributed either to disinterest or to an unwillingness to engage
This does not appear to be the case for this segment of our student population
Instead, there was a noticeable disparity between their level of effort and knowledge gains
The final cluster to emerge at posttest is what we call the Nonstrategic-Reader profile (« = 120)
As this name implies, this cluster distinguished itself by exerting the least amount of strategic effort during studying, as documented by their reported strategy use
Understandably, it was also this group who, on average, remembered the least from the knowledge and motivation passages that they read
Still, this low strategy and recall performance was balanced by moderate outcomes on the domain knowledge and analogical reasoning tasks
Addition- ally, those in the Nonstrategic-Reader cluster claimed to be at least moderately interested in the domain of educational psychology
This contrasting profile leads us to question whether these students were somehow limited in their ability to learn from exposition
On the other hand, are those in this particular cluster the superficial learners thatRenkl (1997) described in his research
That is, it could be that these students' reported interest in the domain did not translate into a willingness to study and recall domain-related information presented within demanding exposition
The fact that this cluster contained the largest number of students at the conclusion of the semester definitely gives us pause

This profile also has implications for students* academic development, consider- ing that learning still depends heavily on the individuals' ability to acquire information from written text (Alexander & Knight, 1993; Alexander & Kulikowich, 1991)

In a related cluster-analytic study, Lorch, Lorch, and Klusewitz (1993) raised similar concerns about the number of under- graduates who seemingly lacked the strategic ability re- quired to comprehend demanding domain exposition

For instance, what happened to those students who began the semester with a high level of interest, a moderate level of knowledge, and a willingness and ability to study and learn from expository text

If this were the case, then we would expect to see a large portion of those students in the pretest Learning- Oriented cluster as members of the Learning-Oriented cluster at posttest
Also, we were interested in those students who fell into the Low-Profile cluster at pretest
Because no clusters were similarly low on all cognitive and motivational dimensions at posttest, it is evident that change did occur during the course of the semester
To address these questions, we tracked the movement of all 329 students from pretest to posttest in terms of then- cluster membership
As this discussion unfolds, it is important to remember that this analysis should be viewed as explor- atory
We also ran chi-square tests, to ascertain whether these movements were beyond the chance level, which they were, x2(3, 329) > 15.65,p < .013
What we determined was that almost 40% of the students characterized as Learning Oriented at pretest were Learning Oriented at posttest
Approximately one quarter of Learning-Oriented students at pretest, however, found their way into either the Effortful-Processor cluster (26%) or the Nonstrategic- Reader group (26%)
This suggests that a substantial portion of those who began with laudable goals again demonstrated a disposition to work hard at learning
Yet they were unable to convert this effort into a high level of subject-matter knowledge

On the other hand, an equivalent number of those students with high interest and initial effortfulness found their way into the cluster distinguished by their inability or unwillingness to learn from demanding text

By and large, the participants who constituted the Low- Profile cluster at pretest tended to find their way into the Nonstrategic-Reader group (40%), followed by the Learning- Oriented (25%) and the Effortful Processor (24%) clusters
Consequently, it appears that all these low-low students in the Low-Profile cluster garnered something from the semes- ter of instruction

The largest percentage acquired a base of educational psychology knowledge and an increased interest in the domain but not the ability or willingness to gain information from demanding text (Nonstrategic Reader)
Others from this cluster ended the semester with relatively high interest in the domain that was reflected also in their studying behavior (Effortful Processor)
Still, their ability to acquire a base of domain knowledge comparable to their peers was limited
One quarter of those with a consistently low profile at the outset of the term turned in a consistently high performance at its conclusion (Learning Oriented), which is encouraging indeed
Finally, the students we described as Strong Knowledge at pretest were, in many ways, the least stable cluster members
The greatest percentage of this group (46%) was ranked among those who had substantial knowledge and some interest but not the ability or the desire to learn from text (Nonstrategic Reader)

Thus, it would seem that begin- ning an introductory course in a domain with relatively moreknowledge than one's peers is not a clear path to high knowledge, personal investment, or strategic capability
Conclusion and Implications Three questions, dealing with the nature, consistency, and malleability of academic profiles, guided this investigation

The principal limitation in addressing these questions rests in our inability to make any definitive statements about the effects of the course instruction on the clusters we character- ized or the shifts in profiles that we documented

It is logical to assume that this shared experience in the form of explicit instruction in domain-related concepts and general strategies would have some impact on students' knowledge, interest, and strategic processing
This seems particularly true be- cause our measures were specific to the domain of educa- tional psychology
However, the absence of controls con- strains our ability to ascribe causality
Thus, our results must be judged as exploratory and require later confirmation or refutation

Likewise, we recognize that the validity of cluster analysis relies on the quality of the measures used to build the profiles, as well as the identification of a psychometri- cally sound criterion against which these profiles can be evaluated (Milligan & Cooper, 1987)

Although we have labored to produce sound indicators of domain knowledge, interest, and strategic processing, alternative measures or the choice of other constructs may have resulted in varied groupings
Despite these potential shortcomings, we believe that this study contributes to the literature on learning and instruction in several important ways
Particularly notewor- thy is a glimpse into the character of intraindividual differences (Ackerman, in press)
First, as it pertains to the nature of academic profiles, this study amplified that success in instructional settings entails the orchestration of cognitive and noncognitive factors
Knowledge, interest, or strategic ability alone did not ensure optimal academic performance

Although an ad- equate base of domain knowledge, of all the variables that we investigated, did contribute to higher performance, its power weakened over time without a concomitant interest in the domain and without the capability to learn from formi- dable exposition
Second, we were struck by the relative consistency in the profiles we uncovered with those described in the literature
The fact that the participants and the domain in the present study varied markedly from those researched by others makes such consistency even more meaningful
Thus, this consistency adds greater credence to the patterns observed in this study
What those patterns reveal is that there generally appears to be two paths to academic success, at least in the initial stages of formal learning
The first, less superlative road is one in which learners, who have somehow acquired a base of relevant knowledge, rely extensively on that knowl- edge to propel their performance

The second path, and one that results in even higher levels of overall achievement, combines knowledge with a personal investment in the learning process, as evidenced by strong interest in the content and strategic effort
